schools.summary: Gill hears the diseased breath grown strange and disagreeable, the word carrying the sense of a woman's travail-pangs; yet allows 'my spirit' (vital spirits spent) or 'my mind' (soul overwhelmed with the terrors of God).

Keil and Delitzsch fix chubbal as 'corrupted, troubled,' the breath grown short and offensive, announcing decay; Ellicott refers it to elephantiasis (margin 'my spirit is consumed'), and reads the plural 'graves' as the Hebrew plural for the singular.
Henry hears a man correcting his earlier 'few years' (ch. 16:22): now already setting out, days extinct like a candle burnt to the socket, the graves of his fathers ready.
Wesley takes 'graves' as the sepulchres of the fathers, a bed soon made; Clarke renders 'my spirit is oppressed' and points to the burial-niches ('sepulchral cells') of an ancient cemetery.

debates.question: Does 'my breath is corrupt' mean the diseased, offensive breath, or 'my spirit is oppressed/consumed'?

sides.position: the literal diseased and offensive breath of a dying man

themes: the graves are ready for me
nothing left to wish for but a grave

schools.summary: Gill takes the 'mockers' not as profane scoffers but as Job's own friends, whom he felt to scorn his misery; hence he begs his cause be heard.

Wesley: do not my friends, instead of comforting, mock me? (returning to ch. 16:20); Clarke marshals the many renderings (Vulgate, LXX, Good, Calmet, Coverdale) and concludes the general sense is plain enough.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'mockery surrounds me... mine eye shall loiter over their disputings,' defending the chapter-division and the chiastic movement; Ellicott glosses 'mine eye continue in their provocation' as a bitter reproach — it can see nothing else.
Henry draws out the sting: the friends provoked Job then condemned his resentment, so his eye 'continued in their provocation' — unkindness enough to try the patience even of Job.

outliers.note: Catalogues the wide spread of renderings the verse has borne (Vulgate, Septuagint, Good, Calmet, Coverdale, Heath) before dismissing the difficulty: 'the general meaning is plain, and the reader has got translations enough.'

themes: are there not mockers with me
the eye fixed on their provocation
mocked by those who came to mourn

schools.summary: Gill reads it spoken to God — 'put, I pray thee, a pledge,' that God would provide a surety and admit one to plead, or set his mind to Job's case.
Ellicott: Job asks God to be surety for him with Himself — the prayer of Hezekiah (Isa. 38:14) and the psalmist (Ps. 119:122); a witness of God to God, language fitting the persons of the Godhead.

Clarke hears the words flung at the friends — 'deposit a pledge, stake your conduct against mine, let the cause come before God'; Wesley keeps the appeal to God to be his surety, 'strike hands' the usual gesture.
Henry grounds it in a clear conscience's boldness toward God, and records the English annotations' glance at Christ the Mediator and surety of the better testament (Heb. 7:22; Rom. 8:32-33).

debates.question: Is the plea for a surety addressed to God or flung at the friends?

sides.position: addressed to God (or Christ the Mediator) to be surety for Job
flung at the friends — deposit a pledge, stake your conduct against mine

outliers.note: Records the English annotations' reading that Job glances at Christ, 'my surety with thee, namely Christ who is with thee in heaven,' the surety of the better testament (Heb. 7:22).

themes: put me in a surety with thee
who will strike hands with me
surety from God or wager to the friends

schools.summary: Gill takes it as a real withholding — God hides understanding naturally, spiritually, and even the meaning of his providences (from Asaph, Jeremiah, Habakkuk), and here from Job's friends, who mistook his case.

Clarke: God does what he only permits, and 'shalt thou not exalt them' was fulfilled — the friends condemned till Job interceded; Wesley: 'thou hast blinded my friends, therefore I desire a wiser judge,' and thou wilt make them ashamed.
Ellicott fixes 'their heart' as the friends' heart; Keil and Delitzsch take God without question as the subject who has both darkened the friends and made Job a byword.

debates.question: What does 'therefore shalt thou not exalt them' foretell?

sides.position: a prophecy of the friends' humbling, fulfilled when God condemned them till Job interceded
a denial of the victory in the contest — God will make them ashamed of their confidence

themes: thou hast hid their heart from understanding
God permits what he is said to do

schools.summary: Gill takes 'flattery to his friends' of the comforters, who flattered Job with promises of prosperity or spoke deceitfully for God; the failing children's eyes are the curse such treachery entails.
Henry reckons the friends among the flatterers — Eliphaz opening with commendation (ch. 4:3), all promising happiness on their terms — flattery designed to vex him.
Clarke owns the great variety of meaning and reaches for the general sense: he who expects much from friends will be disappointed, his children's eyes failing while he leans on them.
Ellicott lays the obscurity open — literally 'for a portion he will tell friends' — offering 'he denounceth his friends for a prey' or the surety-sharing sense, the sons' eyes failing to see it.

debates.question: Whose children's eyes fail — the false friend's posterity, or the deserted man's own?

sides.position: a curse on the flatterer's house for betraying friendship
the disappointment of the man deserted by friends, on his own children

themes: the eyes of the children fail
one of the chapter's darkest cruxes
empty friendship in the day of need

schools.summary: Gill notes Job's name become a proverb (for poverty or patience) but here to his reproach, the byword men use of a wicked man or hypocrite.
Henry hears a fallen favourite — ballads made of him, 'as poor as Job' — and reads 'tabret' two ways: one publicly played upon, or the darling of the race (deliciae humani generis).

Keil and Delitzsch reject the Topheth/hell guess and derive tuph 'to spit out' (onomatopoetic, cf. Arabic for contempt): 'one in whose face they spit'; Ellicott offers either a 'drum openly' as a signal of warning or 'an open abhorrence, one in whose face they spit.'
Clarke denies 'tabret' is the Hebrew; reading liphnehem for lephanim he renders 'I shall be as a furnace, or consuming fire, before them' — Job's example a fire to confound his false friends.

debates.question: What does the disputed word rendered 'as a tabret' mean?

sides.position: a timbrel publicly played upon, or the darling of the race
'one in whose face they spit,' from tuph, to spit out
a drum or tabret openly, a signal of warning to others
a furnace or consuming fire before them (reading liphnehem)

themes: spat upon or set as a warning

schools.summary: Gill keeps the plain cause: the eye grown dim through excessive weeping, the eyesight well-nigh lost.
Clarke: continual weeping impairs the sight, and any wasting affliction weakens the eyes; 'all my members are as a shadow' — nothing left but skin and bone, the shadow of his former self.
Henry gathers a portrait of a man of sorrows — wept almost blind (ch. 16:16), the sorrow of the world working darkness and death, the flesh fretted away to a skeleton, the shadow of a man.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the sense in their rendering, 'mine eye became dim with grief, and all my members were like a shadow,' before the astonishment of the upright.

themes: mine eye dim by reason of sorrow

schools.summary: Gill reads the astonishment as the wonder of sincere men, then and in ages to come, that so good a man should be so afflicted and his friends add to his grief — scarce believable, harder still to account for.

Henry deepens the paradox (a remarkable saint a remarkable sufferer) but hears it animate, not deter: the innocent stirs against the hypocrite, withstanding the scoffer and the profane inferences drawn from Job's case.

Clarke reads it prophetically — the upright astonished, hypocrites unmasked, innocent men shown God's favourites; Wesley: astonied at the depth of God's judgments on innocent men, yet the more zealously opposing the hypocrites.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'the upright were astonished... the innocent is stirred up over the godless,' setting the strophe's truth: the righteous, though he see destruction before him, does not forsake God.

themes: the innocent stirred against the hypocrite
the offence of a suffering saint

schools.summary: Gill defines the righteous man — really so, justified by the living Redeemer's righteousness, living by faith — and sets his holding-on against going back, turning aside, or standing still; a real progress nothing can move.

Henry: the righteous holds on the more constantly ('none of these things move him,' Acts 20:24) and grows stronger by others' trials and his own — the blustering wind makes the traveller gird his cloak the faster.

Clarke makes it the grand use of the book: Job's case illustrates every partial-seeming providence, so none is stumbled to see a godly man oppressed; the righteous counts all well managed and gains strength by every blast.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain triumph: 'the righteous holdeth fast on his way, and he that hath clean hands waxeth stronger and stronger.'

themes: the righteous holds on his way

schools.summary: Gill hears a man confident of his cause daring all three to renew the dispute, or calling them to retract their censures and at least hear him out.

Henry takes it as Job's verdict on their folly — not one wise man who can explain providence or apply the promises; those comfort unwisely who fetch comfort from mere possibility of recovery, not from what cannot fail.
Clarke sharpens the rebuke — the friends too proud to profit, bidden to go again to school for humility and knowledge; Wesley reads an even invitation to renew the debate they were resolved to renew.
Ellicott catches the irony and fixes the last clause as a plain future — 'and I shall not find' a wise man, if ye renew it — Job willing to hear but confident of the result.

outliers.note: Reads the renewed invitation as ironical — 'come again and renew the argument, but I shall not find a wise man among you' — and corrects the tense to a future, 'I shall not find,' rather than a present verdict.

themes: do ye return and come now
not one wise man among you

schools.summary: Gill: not that Job's days outran God's bound, but that in his own apprehension the term of life was spent (folly to promise him long days), or his days of prosperity were past and evil days come.

Wesley: 'I am a dying man, so your hopes of bettering my condition are vain,' the broken purposes those formed for himself and his children; Clarke hears a relapse into gloom, the frequent transitions marking piety's struggle with affliction.

Henry opens all Job had designed — enlarging his border, settling his children, promoting religion, relieving the poor — now cut off; the period of our days ends our worldly contrivances, yet cleaving to the Lord death breaks not that purpose.
Keil and Delitzsch render the purposes as 'the cherished thoughts of my heart' cut off, the possessions of the inner man, and carry on into the friends' false comfort.

themes: the cherished thoughts of the heart
only the purpose fixed on God survives

schools.summary: Gill offers both: Job's own thoughts making the night as broad day for want of sleep, or the friends putting day before night against nature, promising days brighter than noon (ch. 11:17) as death's night comes on.

Wesley: his thoughts so pursue him he can sleep neither by night nor day, the daylight gone as soon as begun for the pains; Clarke renders 'the light is near from the face of darkness' — light scarcely severed from the dark, a mind overcast but for a gleam of hope.

Ellicott reads a bitter comment on the friends, who would have Job believe his night the reverse of darkness, 'the light near unto the darkness,' prosperity close by — the more painful mockery to one whose condition was all dark.

sides.position: the friends, with their false promise that light is near

themes: they change the night into day
the light near unto the darkness

schools.summary: Gill: Job casts no 'if' on waiting upon God, but sets it against the friends' counsel — should he wait for their promised peaceable tabernacle, how soon over, for what house but the grave, man's long home?

Wesley: waiting for deliverance he would be disappointed, on the borders of the grave, making the bed easy by a pure conscience, seeing Christ in it (a bed of spices), looking to the resurrection; Clarke: long life or short, the grave is his home, hope for nothing else.

Henry dwells on the grave till it is almost welcome — a house, to the wicked a prison (ch. 24:19-20), to the godly a passage-house home; a bed to rest in till the everlasting morning (Isa. 57:2), making good people willing to die.

Gill takes 'corruption' as the grave's putrefaction ('pit of corruption'), not the corruptible seed or the boils' matter; as a house holds a family, the grave holds corruption, dust, and worms, with whom Job claims kindred familiarly and respectfully.

Henry: Job cries to corruption 'thou art my father' (bodies formed of earth) and to the worms 'my mother and sister' (man a worm, ch. 21:26); his kindred estranged (ch. 19:13-14), he claims the relations that will cleave when those disown him.

Clarke: 'I came from a corrupted stock and must go to corruption again,' rendering 'to the ditch I have called, Thou art my father'; Wesley glosses 'the pit of corruption, the grave,' which will receive and keep him as parents their children.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the cry in rendering — 'I cry to corruption: Thou art my father; to the worm: Thou art my mother and sister' — a man who has made the grave his family.

themes: the worm my mother and sister

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes: not the grace of hope (an anchor never lost), nor its object (eternal glory), but the hope of outward restoration the friends pressed, which now had no ground left in him.

Wesley: the hope meant is 'the happiness you would have me expect'; Clarke: in such circumstances of what use is hope? were he to expect future good, who could see it realized? — no wonder he complains.

Henry holds the two hopes apart most sharply: not hopeless, but his hope out of sight — 'if in this life only I had hope, most miserable' — the living Redeemer (ch. 19:25), things not seen and eternal, not the perishing comforts of the friends.

themes: the grace of hope not lost

schools.summary: Gill: Job, his friends, and their urged hopes go down together to the grave to lie barred and locked till he who has the keys of death shall loose them; or 'the bars' are the body's bones, going down to rottenness — 'what is my strength, that I should hope?'

Wesley marks the shift from singular hope to plural (as the poetical books do), the 'bars' the innermost parts of the pit; all shortly under the bars till the resurrection, where good men rest together — a foresight to cool contenders; Clarke plays over 'bars' (branches, claws) — the grave a gripping monster or a catacomb's niches — and laments the shadow over minds before Christ brought life and immortality to light.

Ellicott owns this the most difficult verse: 'bars of the pit' masculine but the verb feminine plural, and 'hope' feminine singular — neither agrees; some render 'it shall go down' against grammar; he forces no solution, leaving a cry of utter despair, Job's only rest in the dust.

outliers.note: Owns the verse the most difficult of the chapter, laying open the grammatical knot — the masculine 'bars of the pit' against a feminine-plural verb, with 'hope' (feminine singular) no better a subject — and declines to force a solution.

themes: the hardest verse of the chapter
hopes buried yet the buried raised
